newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Alliance bides its time on acqusitions.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Alliance bides its time on acqusitions.

text.p: Alliance & Leicester, the British building society-turned bank, posted its first set of results as a publicly listed company on Friday and confirmed it was on the lookout for acquisitions.

A&L reported a three percent fall in first-half, pre-tax profits to 178 million pounds ($283 million), ahead of market forecasts. The number included a 28 million pound charge for the costs of conversion.
It said it was not going to be rushed into an acquisition, and ruled out an overseas purchase.

At its half-year results last week rival Woolwich Plc described UK acquisitions as problematic and said it might "cherry-pick" in France where it already has a foothold and where valuations are lower.
A&L, which became a bank on flotation in April, said its acquisition strategy was based on acquiring either more customers or more products to sell to existing customers.
The bank has no interest in investing shareholders money overseas, finance director Richard Pym said.
Returning cash to shareholders remained an option, Pym said, but he refused to committed to a timetable.
He pointed to first half results as showing there was capacity for organic growth and lower capital ratios.
Management was committed to liberating the value of the business but it was still too early to be talking about share buybacks, he added.
"We have a lot of thinking and a lot of planning to do before we get to that stage."
A&L shares gave a positive response to the results, adding 12-1/2 pence to 625.
Underlying operating profits rose seven percent to 206 million pounds.
The dividend was raised by 18 percent to 6.4 pence per share, representing around one third of the expected dividend for the year.
A&L said it expected continued strong competition for the remainder of 1997 and higher interest rates.
While the company has seen some outflow of business since its conversion in April, in the last few weeks windfall withdrawals have fallen significantly.
Overall, customer accounts were almost identical to year-end -- less than 100 million pounds lower at 18.1 billion pounds.
Net mortgage lending increased sharply to 527 million pounds from 131 million pounds last year, a market share of 4.5 percent.
But the company cautioned that competition in both the core mortgage and savings markets had continued to put pressure on interest margins.
Mortgages and investments contributed 128 million pounds to group operating profits up six million pounds on last year.

The cost/income ratio of the mortgage and investments business, excluding conversion costs, fell to 45.3 percent from 48.2 percent in first half 1996, underlining the continuing commitment to improving the group's operating efficiency, it said.
Staff reductions will continue in the second half though not at the rate in the first six months. In the past year, underlying staff levels have fallen by 10 percent.
Jobs would continue to go in a number of areas but the group is also building numbers in insurance and leasing.
A&L recently launched in its own general insurance business which will be a core part of the product portfolio going forward.
The group will selectively take some underwriting positions to test the market and, with a collection mechanism for premiums - its branch network, it believes it has a competitive advantage.
Girobank produced level profit for the first half and the strategy remains to develop business within Girobank by selling specialist banking products to its existing customer base.
Last November it bought Sovereign Finance - a leasing business and A&L intends to leverage that by selling leases into existing Girobank commercial customers.
($ = 0.628 British Pounds)
